items.abstract_text: Task switching is a well-established paradigm for assessing cognitive flexibility. However, the precise role of inhibition in task switching remains unclear. This study investigates the effects of inhibition on switch costs in tasks requiring participants to judge whether the magnitude (small vs. large) or parity (odd vs. even) of a number was the same as that presented in previous trials. To this end, an n-back task was embedded in the task-switching paradigm. The results of Experiment 1 demonstrated that, in comparison to the 1-back condition, switch costs were significantly reduced in the 2-back condition, which involved an increased inhibition process. The selective increase in inhibition in some trials in the 1-back condition (Experiment 2) and the carryover of inhibition (Experiment 3) significantly reduced the switch costs. These findings indicate that the enhanced inhibition of task-irrelevant information can facilitate cognitive flexibility in task switching and reduce switch costs, providing novel empirical evidence for the inhibition mechanism underlying task switching.

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 (
                       P 
                       < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 (
                       P 
                       = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47;
                       P 
                       < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21;
                       P 
                       < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group (
                       P 
                       = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group (
                       P 
                       < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43;
                       P 
                       < 0.001).
                     
                   
                   
                     Conclusions 
                     AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

items.abstract_text:
VANFROG.ART is an artistic research project exploring how artificial intelligence, digital image-making, play and audience participation can encourage renewed attention to art. The project centres on two recurring characters: René VANFROG, a frog who enters and interacts with well-known artworks, and Julie, a shy duckling who hides within them. Through a daily participatory game, viewers are invited to find Julie, transforming observation from passive viewing into an active and playful experience.The research investigates whether this simple mechanism can extend the time and quality of attention devoted to an artwork, while creating a dialogue between historical art, contemporary digital practices and artificial intelligence. The project combines artistic reinterpretation, visual storytelling, social-media participation and an educational component, “L’Angolo del Prof”, which introduces artists, techniques, historical contexts and curiosities.Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a substitute for artistic thought, VANFROG.ART approaches it as a creative tool within a human-directed process. The project examines how play, participation and AI-assisted image-making can generate new forms of engagement with existing artistic heritage and stimulate curiosity, visual attention and artistic literacy. 
                 keywords: artistic research, artificial intelligence, participatory art, visual attention, art education, digital art, gamification

items.abstract_text: This exploration examines the impact of supplementary AI-generated explanatory materials on foundational mathematics learning and creative metacognition in primary education. The study followed a quantitative, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with a nonequivalent control group. Fourth-grade classes in five schools were assigned to conditions at the classroom level: an intervention group receiving AI-facilitated handouts (n = 135) and a control group using programmatic textbooks (n = 128). Students in the experimental condition received eight supplementary lessons featuring paper-based handouts. These handouts presented explanations, examples, and illustrations of new mathematical topics generated by a large language model (Gemini 2.5 Pro), prompted the inclusion of age-appropriate content and a dedicated section encouraging creative metacognition (reflection and novel idea generation). Baseline equivalence was confirmed. The outcomes assessed included single-digit mental arithmetic, multidigit calculation, arithmetic word problem-solving, and creative metacognition, which were analyzed via multilevel or robust linear modeling accounting for classroom clustering. The results indicated no statistically significant differences between groups on single-digit mental arithmetic tasks. However, students who received AI-generated materials showed significantly greater improvement in multidigit calculation tasks and one-step word problem-solving than did the control group. No significant difference was found for multistep word problems. The intervention group also presented a substantially greater increase in creative metacognition scores than did the control group. The findings provide preliminary quasi-experimental evidence that curated, static AI-generated explanations, when designed to include metacognitive prompts, may be associated with greater gains in specific procedural and applied mathematical skills and creative metacognition among fourth-grade students under the conditions studied. This approach illustrates how generative AI can be leveraged as an authoring tool to supplement standard instruction and cultivate higher-order cognitive skills in young learners.

items.abstract_text: Background: Invasive natured medical procedures, such as venipuncture and intravenous cannulation, are sources of acute pain as well as here to distress in pediatric populations, particularly among preschoolers in this way. Unmanaged aspects here are to send procedural pain leads to heightened anxiety as well as needle phobias. Non-pharmacological interventions, specifically distraction techniques, are mostly recommended. While traditional distraction methods have here to be proven effective, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced novel interventions, such as herein AI-adaptive virtual reality (VR). Objective: This study aims here to assess as well as compare the effectiveness of AI-assisted distraction versus traditional based distraction on procedural pain as well as anxiety during invasive procedures among preschoolers (aged 3–6). Methods: A randomized, three-arm clinical trial was here by conducted in a pediatric outpatient setting. A total of 150 preschoolers requiring natured venipuncture were assigned to one of three groups: AI-Assisted Distraction (n=50), Traditional Distraction (cartoon watching and bubble blowing, n=50), or a Control Group (standard care, n=50). Pain was evaluated using the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) scale as well as the Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale. Anxiety was hereby measured using the Children's Fear Scale (CFS). Results: The AI-Assisted Distraction group hereby exhibited significantly lower FLACC scores (Mean = 2.14, SD = 1.05) compared to both of the Traditional group (Mean = 3.82, SD = 1.34) as well as the Control group (Mean = 6.45, SD = 1.52) (p < 0.001). FACES scores followed a similar trend. Conclusion: AI-assisted structure here to be distraction is significantly more effective than traditional distraction in reducing natured procedural pain and anxiety among preschoolers.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Children today grow up in a hybrid physical and digital environment, engaging with mobile devices from an early age, which poses a risk of negatively impacting their development. This usage often replaces social interactions and physical activities, potentially deteriorating relationships, socio-cognitive skills, and mental health. Banning device use is unrealistic, but the way children use mobiles can be altered through responsible technology. In the present study we (1) explored parental expectations regarding children’s mobile applications, (2) directlyincorporated these expectations into the design of a specific application (Alphie), and (3) examined its reception through UX testing. Alphie is a child-focused application (launcher) that promotes social interaction, real-world activities, and reduces solitary screen time. Its design is informed by parental expectations and scientific data, emphasizing educational, age-appropriate, and moderately stimulating content, with parental control features. A user study with parent-child dyads showed positive experiences. Notably, the games requiring active parental involvement were also well-received, suggesting that they are effective tools for facilitating joint activities within the family. This research highlights how responsible technology can support the mental and physical health of the new generation. By linking parental expectations, application design, and user experience within a single framework, the present studyprovides a more integrative perspective on the development and evaluation of child-focused digital applications.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Parents and children participated in a longitudinal study investigating whether different personality versions of Alphie influence children's social interactions and sociocognitive skills differently. For the present UX study, we analyzed only the responses to the questionnaire in which parents and children rated how much they liked Alphie's games. We received 31 responses from children aged between 6.3 and 8.8 years (M ± SD = 7.5 ± 0.7); 16 were girls (sex assigned at birth). The age range was narrower than our previously defined 4-9-year-old target group due to additional socio-cognitive measurements that required a more homogeneous sample. Thirty parents completed the questionnaire; all identified as women (although both parents were eligible to participate). Regarding educational background, 4 had vocational/high school degrees, 14 held bachelor's degrees, and 12 had master's degrees. Four families lived in the capital, 6 in other large cities, 11 in smaller towns, and 9 in villages. Data were collected between August and October 2023. After children had used Alphie for one month, parents were asked to complete the UX questionnaire online. Following this, we arranged online video calls via Microsoft Teams with both the parent and child present. During these meetings (which also included tests of socio-cognitive skills, e.g., false belief test; not discussed here), the experimenter read aloud the UX questions to the child and recorded the child's responses directly into the online questionnaire. These interviews and the filling out of the questionnaires for the parents lasted approximately 10 min. All personal data were anonymized, and the study complied with ethical standards. It was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the United Ethical Review Committee for Research in Psychology (EPKEB; approval number: 2022/101). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

However, although there are tens or hundreds of thousands of applications on the market that claim to be educational (Healthy Children 2018) , their real educational potential and effectiveness are often low (Taylor et al. 2022) . Additionally, they rarely offer age-appropriate language or guidance (Callaghan and Reich 2018; Taylor et al. 2022) . Therefore, parents' expectations about being educational and age-appropriate are often not met. Apps usually also contain advertisements (unless a subscription is paid). In addition to the financial risks (e.g., children unintentionally charge the parents' bank account), these ads often appear in the form of pop-up windows, which may distract attention and decrease children's engagement with the app (Meyer et al. 2021) . Related to this, overstimulation is considered harmful to children's attention and executive function by researchers ( Christakis et al. 2012, 2018 Parents did not spontaneously express a need to be actively involved in their child's device use. In contrast, they think that an ideal app for children should contain both entertaining and educational content, which the child can use easily, implying that they prefer the child to be able to engage independently and use the content autonomously. This is in line with a finding that, when choosing an app, the most important need for parents is "independent entertainment", i.e., need for their child to have fun, to understand the app, and to be able to use it independently (Broekman et al. 2016 ). However, the second most important need was labelled as "co-education", and reflected parents' desire for their children to learn from an app, while also having the ability to control or co-use it with them (Broekman et al. 2016) . In accordance with this, in our study, parents quite liked the idea of such apps/games that would need their engagement: the digital board game that would suggest and facilitate real-world activities for the children and their parents, and the story creator in which children and parents would be able to create their own stories with the help of images, texts and advice. Therefore, parents might not be reluctant to engage in the child's device use if we offer them entertaining ways of doing this. It remains an open question whether increasing parental awareness of the benefits of joint media engagement would increase their willingness to engage in co-use with their children. Parents also found important that an app for children should encourage physical activity. Given the increasing prevalence of obesity in industrialized societies, this is undoubtedly in line with professional and scientific principles. Research shows the positive effects of exergames on both physical activity (Staiano and Calvert 2011) and cognitive functions (Best 2012; Benzing and Schmidt 2019; Gashaj et al. 2021) . However, there is a need to develop exergames for mobile devices instead of console games, as mobile devices are more common and more easily used by younger children. In conclusion, parents expressed positive attitudes towards those goals we aim to achieve with Alphie, both in open-ended and focused, close-ended questions. They also liked the specific game ideas we described: in most cases, they gave an average of 4 out of 5 points on a scale expressing their level of liking. These findings directly informed the design features of Alphie. For example, the parental preference for ad-free and educational content motivated the inclusion of carefully selected cognitive games without external advertisements. In addition to scientific considerations, parental concerns about overstimulation reinforced our decision to use minimal animations and sounds. Most notably, the strong parental interest in apps that encourage joint activities reinforced our decision to develop Alphie's story-creating game and the cooperative boardgame, both of which were positively received in the parental survey. While most games were rated positively, there was some variation in ratings. Children particularly liked Tic-Tac-Toe, the Balloon-Popping Game, the Colors and Shapes Game, the Board Game, and the Multiplayer Drawing Game. They rated the Story-Creating Game, the Picture-Matching Game, and the Etch-a-Sketch Game lower. The latter two may have posed challenges: the Picture-Matching Game may demand high executive function and attention, while the Etch-a-Sketch requires fine motor skills. These factors might have contributed to their lower ratings, although this interpretation should be examined in future research. The lower rating of the Story-Creating Game is more surprising, especially since parents liked it more and had previously expressed interest in such a game during Study 1 (parental survey). As our fundamental aim with this game is to encourage parents to tell stories to the child, it is important that parents like it enough to use it regularly. Children might have liked this game a bit less because they might have tried to play it independently, although it is not designed for solo use. More detailed user experience studies are needed to understand why children like these games less, and inform further development. The Board game was well-liked by both parents and children, aligning with the results of Study 1 (parental survey). Therefore, this game appears to be a valuable tool for facilitating joint activities in the family, encouraging parental involvement in the children's mobile devices use, and promoting real-world engagement, including physical activity. Although it's unclear whether parents rated the games based on direct experience or observation, the high ratings for Mastermind, Color Sudoku, and Tangram suggest that these games appeal to adults as well (probably because advanced levels can also be chosen). The relatively low standard deviations (high agreement among parents) in Study 1 (closed-ended questions) may also reflect socially desirable responding. items.abstract_text: Promotion has always been a problem of attention: a firm must decide what to say, to whom, and at which moment. Artificial intelligence now participates in each of those decisions. This paper reviews how machine learning, generative models, and predictive systems have been built into promotional practice, and what scholarly and trade evidence reveals about their results. It organizes the technology into five working capabilities, follows them through six commercial settings, and examines four cases drawn from music streaming, food manufacturing, financial services, and ride hailing. It then considers how returns are measured, why outcomes differ so sharply between firms, and which risks deserve closest attention: privacy erosion, skewed ad delivery, undisclosed synthetic media, sameness of creative output, and upheaval in marketing careers. The central argument is that AI produces its strongest promotional results when it is treated as an organizational capability, supported by sound data, clear accountability, and human review, rather than as software that can simply be purchased and switched on.

items.abstract_text: Guided by Griffiths’ components model of addiction and the I-PACE (Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution) framework, this study tested whether psychological distress is associated with Facebook addiction and smartphone orientation through two emotion-regulation pathways: fear of missing out (FoMO) and escapism. A cross-sectional sample of N = 480 adults (86.3% female, 11.7% male) completed measures of psychological distress, FoMO, escapism, Facebook addiction, and smartphone orientation. Structural equation modeling was used to compare mediation models linking these variables. Psychological distress was not directly associated with Facebook addiction (β = 0.01, nonsignificant), but it was positively related to FoMO (β = 0.49) and escapism (β = 0.38). FoMO (β = 0.46) and escapism (β = 0.09) were both associated with Facebook addiction. Facebook addiction (β = 0.21), FoMO (β = 0.32), and escapism (β = 0.26) were associated with smartphone orientation. Model comparisons showed that the full mediation model was the most parsimonious and best-fitting representation of the data. Psychological distress appears to be linked to problematic Facebook use and smartphone orientation indirectly, primarily through FoMO and secondarily through escapism. Interventions may therefore benefit from targeting FoMO and maladaptive escapist coping rather than distress alone.

items.title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
items.abstract_text: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The development and ubiquitous availability of large language model based systems (LLMs) poses a plurality of potentials and risks for education in schools and universities. In this paper, we provide an analysis and discussion of the overreliance concern as one specific risk: that students might fail to acquire important skills, or be inhibited in the acquisition of these skills, because they overly rely on LLMs. We use the distinction between local and global goals of education to guide our investigation. In our view, the harm of LLM overreliance is specifically that it severs the connection between local educational goals (e.g., successfully solving a specific kind of math problem) and global educational goals (e.g., acquiring general skills for mathematics). Based on this analysis, we sketch three possible responses to the overreliance concern: preserving both local and global goals while making minimal changes to educational practice (a conservative approach), changing global and local educational goals (a revisionary perspective), and preserving global educational goals while changing local goals (an in-between view). Since different types of responses have different benefits and weaknesses, we think that it is likely that an optimal response ultimately combines elements from all three types.

items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT and Claude have rapidly become everyday tools for hundreds of millions of people. Unlike earlier tools, they do not merely retrieve information but analyse, write and draw conclusions on the user's behalf. This narrative review analyses the available empirical evidence on how offloading cognitive tasks to generative AI affects brain engagement, learning, memory and critical thinking. It focuses on an EEG study from the MIT Media Lab (n=54), a survey of 319 knowledge workers by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University, a randomised field experiment with high-school students and related research. The evidence indicates that uncritical reliance on AI is associated with lower engagement of the user's own cognitive resources during the task, poorer recall of self-written text and a reduced tendency to verify AI output; the higher the trust in AI, the less critical scrutiny is applied. However, the evidence base is still limited: studies are small, some are non-peer-reviewed preprints, and no long-term harm has been demonstrated. A conceptual model of "cognitive debt" accumulation and recommendations for the reasoned use of AI in higher education, including medical education, are proposed.

These technology has not only given a better learning evenvironment, it also creates a certain amount of pressure which results in stress among the students. This study aims to analyse the interrelationships between techno-stress, attention difficulties, psychological effects with cognitive fatigue among the undergraduate students in digital mediated learning environments. Quantitative correlational research was used and grounded on the theories of Cognitive Load Theory and Information Processing Theory. It looked at the cognitive effects and psychological effects of prolonged use of digital devices. The data was collected using a structured questionnaire 121 undergraduate engineering students aged 17–23 years through purposive sampling. The techno-stress, attention and learning difficulties, cognitive fatigue and psychological effects were measured. The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) was used to analyze the data with descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis. As per the results, techno-stress (M = 14.40), cognitive fatigue (M = 13.83), attention-related problems (M = 14.16), and psycho-affective repercussions (M = 14.84 resulted moderate level. Prior research has established a strong correlation between cognitive fatigue and techno-stress, which refers to anxiety and impairment of daily functioning caused by technology disruptions. The study indicates prolonged digital learning overloads students’ brain, exhausts them mentally, makes them inattentive, and induces psychological strain.

items.preview: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical and health-professions education offers opportunities for personalized learning, access to information, and cognitive support, while raising concerns about cognitive offloading and the potential displacement of critical thinking and independent judgment. items.abstract_text: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical and health-professions education offers opportunities for personalized learning, access to information, and cognitive support, while raising concerns about cognitive offloading and the potential displacement of critical thinking and independent judgment. This article presents a conceptual and normative theological-ethical analysis of the responsible integration of AI into health-professions education. It draws on a focused, critical, and integrative review of empirical and theoretical scholarship on AI, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, clinical reasoning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI interaction. The literature is analyzed using the See-Judge-Act method: the See phase identifies contemporary educational tensions associated with AI; the Judge phase evaluates these tensions through Catholic theological anthropology; and the Act phase develops a normative educational framework. The theological analysis draws particularly on Antiqua et Nova, Quo vadis, humanitas?, and Magnifica humanitas, which, respectively, illuminate the distinction between artificial and human intelligence, the embodied, relational, and situated character of human intelligence, and human primacy amid technological development. The analysis results in a human-centered, human-in-the-loop framework in which AI functions as cognitive support while learners retain responsibility for reasoning, judgment, reflection, and decision-making. The framework translates these principles into implications for curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, clinical simulation, AI literacy, and professional formation. As a conceptually derived framework, it has not yet been empirically validated and should therefore be understood as a normative and theoretically grounded proposition for subsequent empirical testing. The article contributes a theological-ethical model for integrating AI in health-professions education while preserving human intelligence, critical formation, and professional responsibility as central aims of education.

items.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) adoption grows in medical education, AI assistants have become important learning support tools for medical students. However, existing research has primarily focused on learning performance and technology adoption, while little is known about how perceived AI assistant intelligence influences medical students' mental health. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study develops a model linking perceived AI assistant intelligence to mental health through the serial mediating roles of learning goal progress and academic anxiety, while examining the moderating role of AI literacy. A two-study design was employed. Study 1 surveyed 721 Chinese medical students, and Study 2 conducted a real human-AI interaction experiment with 398 medical students. Results showed that perceived AI assistant intelligence positively predicts learning goal progress. Learning goal progress and academic anxiety jointly mediate the relationship between perceived AI assistant intelligence and mental health. In addition, AI literacy strengthens the positive effect of perceived AI assistant intelligence on learning goal progress and enhances its indirect effect on mental health through the serial mediation pathway. The experimental findings further support the robustness of these relationships. This study extends research on AI in education by uncovering the psychological mechanisms through which perceived AI assistant intelligence affects medical students' mental health. It also enriches the application of SDT in human-AI collaborative learning contexts and provides practical implications for optimizing AI-assisted learning environments, improving AI literacy, and promoting student well-being.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The rapid pace of Artificial Intelligence (AI) development is posing unprecedented challenges for the organisation of societies and the contemporary legal order. This study explores possible scenarios related to the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, focusing on the balance between socio-economic benefits and existential risks on a planetary scale. Special attention is given to the legal dimensions of new technologies, with the identification of gaps in contemporary legal regulation of algorithmic autonomy. A global legal regulatory framework, grounded in international cooperation, transparency, and the supremacy of human rights, is proposed as a strategic solution. The methodology encompasses prospective scenario analysis and a systematic bibliographic review spanning computer science, ethics, political science, and international law. The analysis distinguishes three prospective scenarios — optimisation and prosperity, misalignment and disruption, and existential risk — and examines the structural challenges AI poses to labour markets, algorithmic justice, and global security. The study concludes that anticipatory, internationally coordinated regulation of new technologies is crucial for ensuring their development remains compatible with human safety, dignity, and long-term collective welfare.

items.title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
items.abstract_text: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by reducing the time and effort required to access information, solve problems, and complete academic tasks. Although these capabilities can improve learning efficiency, their implications for deeper understanding and independent learning remain uncertain. This review examines the cognitive effort paradox in GenAI-supported education: the possibility that reducing unnecessary mental effort can facilitate learning while excessive cognitive delegation may weaken the processes through which knowledge is constructed and retained. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, desirable difficulties, self-regulated learning, and cognitive offloading research, the review distinguishes productive cognitive assistance from cognitive substitution. It examines how GenAI influences cognitive load, learning engagement, metacognitive monitoring, knowledge retention, and independent problem-solving. The synthesis suggests that the educational value of reduced cognitive effort depends on the nature of the task, learner characteristics, instructional design, and whether students remain actively involved in learning-relevant processing. An integrative conceptual framework is proposed to explain the conditions under which GenAI-supported efficiency may strengthen or constrain learning. The review offers directions for experimental research, educational assessment, and responsible GenAI integration in higher education.
